title: Community Colleges Rethink Program Value
summary:
Community Colleges Rethink Program Value
Joshua.Bay Tue, 07/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

An initiative co-created by the Aspen Institute and the Community College Research Center helped 10 colleges move more than 20,000 students into programs leading to jobs and bachelor’s degrees.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Between 2022 and 2025, 10 community colleges moved more than 20,000 additional students into programs that lead to living-wage jobs or bachelor’s degree pathways, according to a new report from the Aspen Institute College Excellence Program and the Community College Research Center.

The findings come as community colleges face growing pressure to demonstrate the value of their credentials. Although more community college students are earning credentials than ever, more than one-third of those credentials are unlikely to lead directly to living-wage jobs or bachelor’s degrees that open doors to them.

To help more students enroll in programs with stronger postgraduation outcomes, Aspen and CCRC launched the Unlocking Opportunity network in 2023. The initiative aims to increase the number of students entering and completing high-value programs while helping colleges improve programs with weaker postcompletion outcomes.

The initiative began with 10 pilot colleges—ranging from large urban institutions to small rural-serving colleges—that collectively serve more than 170,000 students. During the three-year period ending in 2025, those colleges increased enrollment in high-value pathways by 27 percent while reducing enrollment in programs with weaker postcompletion outcomes by 25 percent.

Josh Wyner, executive director of Aspen’s College Excellence Program, which aims to strengthen higher education leadership to improve student success, said the initiative grew out of a long-standing challenge facing community colleges: Too many students were enrolling in programs that did not lead to strong employment or transfer opportunities, while colleges often focused more on getting students through the front door than on what happened after they enrolled.

“When the incentive structure is for colleges to enroll as many students as possible, two things happen: One is colleges spend a lot of time worrying about the front door and think about that often in short-term ways,” Wyner said. “The second is that they pay less attention to what happens to [students] during and after college.”

“What I think people realized, but weren’t paying enough attention to, is that what students were completing didn’t lead to postgraduation success in bachelor’s attainment or in good jobs,” he added.

Rethinking program value: The initiative defines “high-value” programs as those that provide students with stronger economic opportunities after completion. For career-focused programs, value is measured by graduates’ earnings. For transfer pathways, value is measured by transfer rates, bachelor’s degree completion and clear academic avenues between community colleges and four-year institutions.

The report highlights several ways colleges redesigned academic programs to better align with local workforce needs and transfer outcomes. Southwest Wisconsin Technical College launched a radiologic-technology program to meet regional workforce demand, while San Antonio College increased nursing enrollment by 71 percent through expanded employer partnerships. After reviewing student outcomes, Odessa College eliminated its general studies degree and strengthened advising to guide students toward programs with stronger postgraduation results.

Wyner said he didn’t expect such rapid changes.

“What surprised me most is how many students were able to move into high-value programs in such a short period of time,” Wyner said. “I didn’t think enrollments would move that quickly, and at that volume.”

Closing equity gaps: The gains were particularly strong among students of color and lower-income students: Enrollment in high-value programs increased by more than 17,000 students, a 40 percent increase, according to the report.

Wyner said students of color and lower-income students have historically been more likely to enroll in programs with weaker employment and transfer outcomes, making them among the biggest beneficiaries of the initiative.

“If you really work on strengthening program value and advising to get students to make earlier and better decisions, you’re going to disproportionately help those students who otherwise would be most likely to be in the lower-value programs,” Wyner said.

The pilot colleges also increased the number of dual-enrollment students entering structured academic pathways. Compared with the 2022 baseline, more than 6,000 additional dual-enrollment students are now on well-defined educational plans.

Looking ahead: While the early results are encouraging, Wyner said, the initiative’s long-term success will depend on whether more students complete their programs, transfer to four-year institutions and secure higher-paying jobs.

As the initiative continues, Aspen and CCRC plan to track bachelor’s degree attainment and graduates’ earnings to determine whether the enrollment gains translate into better long-term outcomes.

Wyner credited the participating colleges with driving the reforms, noting that Aspen and CCRC provided the analytical framework and coaching, while institutions implemented the changes.

“The ultimate outcome that matters is whether students have thriving lives and fulfilling careers and good jobs,” Wyner said. “I’m encouraged that colleges are signing up to do the work.”

title: Initiative launched to create Campus Biodiversity Registers across colleges, unversities in India
summary: The nationwide exercise to document the flora and fauna within the walls of higher education institutions is anchored by the Nature Conservation Foundation and the National Biodiversity Authority
full_text:
Nature Conservation Foundation (NCF), a Mysuru-based wildlife research and conservation organisation, and the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) have launched an initiative to document biodiversity found within college and university campuses across India.

The objective of the year-long nationwide exercise is to create a Campus Biodiversity Register (CBR) for each higher education institution.

According to the NCF, the CBR has been inspired by the People’s Biodiversity Register (PBR), which contains comprehensive information on locally available bio-resources, including the landscape and demography of a particular area, and traditional knowledge.

“The CBR project enables educational institutions to document the biodiversity found within their campuses. While the PBRs document the biodiversity of villages, towns, and cities, the focus of the CBRs is on educational institutions, bringing together students, faculty, and other staff to explore nature around them,” a statement from the organisation said.

Conservationists have underlined the importance of college and university campuses as green spaces in India’s expanding urban landscape. Many such institutions harbour a diversity of trees, birds, butterflies, insects, reptiles, mammals, fungi, and countless other organisms.

“These campuses often serve as biodiversity hotspots and refuges within urban landscapes, yet surprisingly little is known about the species they support. Without this knowledge, it is difficult to appreciate, conserve and manage these valuable ecosystems,” the statement read.

The organisation said colleges and universities can register for the initiative until November 2026, and the documentation will be concluded in June 2027.

Specific platforms

Over the course of a year, participating institutions will document biodiversity using the recognised platforms iNaturalist, eBird, and SeasonWatch. “Whether through organised biodiversity surveys, campus walks, or everyday observations, participants will record the plants, animals, fungi, and other life forms they encounter. By the end of the project, each institution will have the information, skills and resources needed to compile its own CBR,” the NCF said.

The biodiversity observations generated through the project are envisaged to contribute to global biodiversity databases while also helping institutions better understand and manage their own campuses. The initiative also aims to foster curiosity about the natural world and encourage a deeper connection between students and the biodiversity that surrounds them.

“This is an opportunity to notice the biodiversity that often goes unnoticed geckos on classroom walls, moths around campus lights, ants around us, and countless other organisms that quietly share our campuses,” NCF’s programme manager Devica Ranade said on Tuesday (July 21, 2026).

NBA Chairperson Virendra Tiwary said India’s youth have a crucial role in fulfilling the nation’s commitment to conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity. “Documenting the biodiversity around them is the first step towards conservation,” he said.

title: Student storytellers and creator schemes gain ground in higher education marketing
summary:
As Gen Z and Gen Alpha tune out traditional ads and polished brand messaging, universities and global test providers are turning to student creators, digital ambassadors and peer storytelling to build trust.

The post Student storytellers and creator schemes gain ground in higher education marketing appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Universities and education brands are increasingly formalising student content creator roles, investing in peer‑to‑peer campaigns and experimenting with digital “student ambassador” models to reach prospective learners.

“The new generation is immune to marketing. It’s immune to sales,” Mark Balneger, co‑founder of student creator platform UpperClass, told The PIE News.

For Balneger, the most persuasive “influencers” are already inside institutions.

“The best kind of student creator is either current students or alumni of the university. Those are your best marketing tools,” he argued.

“The amount of followers they have means absolutely nothing.” What counts, he suggested, is credibility inside a specific niche – a business student in Lagos hearing from someone like them at a campus in Toronto; a first‑generation student in Vietnam following another Vietnamese student through the realities of working part‑time in Australia.

Balneger points to conversations that never surface in prospectuses or official webinars.

He describes, for example, a Russian student studying in Korea fielding questions from another Russian student back home: “Is there enough Russian food? Do you experience racism because you’re Russian? Are they judging you because of the Russian‑Ukraine war?”

Those are exactly the issues, he said, that agents, universities or generic influencers are unlikely to address head‑on – but the answers can determine whether a student applies at all.

Many universities already run student ambassador schemes aimed at converting prospects who have shortlisted an institution.

Balneger sees that work as sitting “down the funnel”. According to him, the new wave of student creators, operate much earlier, long before a prospect has joined a mailing list or booked an open day.

Content is shared within “hundreds of small, overlapping circles” of friends, classmates and compatriots, often on personal channels the institution doesn’t see.

“If you have 100 students making content… they post content on their platform, and it spreads in their network,” he explained. “It’s a part of the network that the school cannot touch by posting on their social media.”

Universities from Carleton in Canada to Arizona State in the US and UCL in the UK have already begun formalising these roles, advertising for student storytellers and content creators to produce social, video and written content about campus life.

For those still nervous about giving students a more prominent role in their marketing, Balneger warned them that the shift is already happening without them.

“Students are already posting about your university, but you have no control of it, and you have no way to capitalise on it,” he said.

“You cannot stop them from making content. You cannot sue your students for saying something about your school. They’re already doing it, but now you can structure it, utilise it, work with your students, and capitalise on it.”

You cannot stop them from making content. You cannot sue your students for saying something about your school. They’re already doing it, but now you can structure it, utilise it, work with your students, and capitalise on it

Mark Balneger, UpperClass

For Balneger, this peer‑to‑peer turn is not a passing marketing fad.

“We honestly know that this is the future of higher education marketing – peer to peer, student to student. Students trust students,” he said.

Similar dynamics are starting to reshape how global test providers speak to prospective test takers. ETS, the organisation behind the TOEFL iBT test, has been repositioning the TOEFL brand since it launched an enhanced version of the exam, with a focus on student‑centred storytelling and creator‑driven content.

As part of its transformation, ETS rolled out the ‘Learn It, Take It, Review It’ campaign, inviting 35 influencers, educators and partners in multiple markets to sit the updated test themselves.

Their reactions and reviews were then used in campaign content so that so that students could “see the updated TOEFL iBT test through trusted voices, not just brand messaging”.

“Our goal has been and continues to be that we are aligning the TOEFL experience with the students taking it and the future they are preparing for,” said Omar Chihane, global general manager of TOEFL at ETS.

“Today’s learners expect flexibility, authenticity, and support throughout their journey. TOEFL is evolving to reflect the realities of global mobility, digital learning, and the future of work while continuing to deliver the academic trust institutions rely on.”

Around that creator‑led core, ETS has leaned into formats that look more like youth culture than conventional test prep.

An original anthem and music video, ‘You Speak World’, has been supported by a global social and dance campaign encouraging students to stitch their own content.

Elsewhere, student‑led videos highlight preparation journeys, test‑day experiences and study‑abroad life, while ‘Tina’, a digital student ambassador, frontlines social‑first guidance and tips in a tone closer to a peer than to a corporate account.

title: Long read: Finding international student scholarships in the US – and when to look elsewhere
summary:
As more affordable study destinations emerge as quality education hubs, students are increasingly questioning the ROI of an American degree. Evan Bourtis explores financial aid options for international students in the US.

The post Long read: Finding international student scholarships in the US – and when to look elsewhere appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Sooraj Sahani, an international student from Nepal, remembers the moment when he learned that Texas State University had accepted him on a full scholarship. It meant that he could afford to pursue his dream of becoming a physicist.

For out-of-state students, Texas State can cost up to $25,000 in tuition and roughly $18,000 for housing, food, and other expenses per year. International students must also shoulder costs including health insurance, visa processing fees, and travel expenses. In addition, many international students remain in the US over the summer, meaning housing costs pile up year-round.

Before they get to the US, prospective students must pay $350 in SEVIS fees and $185 in visa application fees – both non-refundable if their visa is rejected. What’s more, the Trump administration is set to bring in a further $250 ‘visa integrity fee’, though this is yet to be implemented.

As such, the total cost of graduating from a US public or private university and living there for four years can exceed $185,000. Because international students don’t qualify for federal aid or federal loans, many have no choice but to pay the full fee. That’s unless they can secure a major scholarship or institutional aid.

Sahani, now a rising junior, went into his freshman year on a full scholarship because of his high grades and standardized test scores. He then secured two more scholarships through the school’s physics department, allowing him to pay for the additional classes beyond the 18-credit limit of a full-time student.

Two Nepalese international students who Sahani lives with also secured large scholarships for Texas State, he said. During his college search, Sahani only considered schools that had scholarship opportunities for international students.

“The most important thing as an international student is to first look into which schools give scholarships and which you might qualify for,” he said.

Scholarships and aid for international students are often competitive and can be hard to find, says Nat Smitobol, a college admissions counsellor at the educational consultancy IvyWise. It costs more for a college to fully fund an international student than a domestic student, because the school doesn’t get any federal support.

Despite that, some colleges give several million dollars a year in international student aid. Wesleyan University in Connecticut provided an average of $90,100 in aid to 108 international students during the 2024 to 2025 school year, topping US News and World Report’s list of schools that gave the most average international aid. Williams College in Massachusetts came in second, with an average of $88,400 in aid for 123 international students, followed by Duke University in North Carolina, with an average of $88,270 for 190 students.

Over half of the schools on the top 20 list are medium-sized liberal arts colleges, which Smitobol said doesn’t surprise him. While international students tend to gravitate toward larger, more well-known universities, these schools have fewer incentives for providing large international aid packages.

“When you’re, let’s say, NYU [New York University] or USC [University of Southern California], you have so much visibility around the world that you don’t really need merit-based scholarship or international aid to attract an applicant pool,” he said. “You can fill the spots with students that aren’t applying for financial aid.”

On the other hand, smaller, less selective colleges often try to attract highly gifted students – international or domestic – to boost their national rankings. The same applies to research universities aiming to boost their global acclaim. If any student has grades and standardised test scores far above the college’s average, it could be an incentive for the college to provide up to a full ride in institutional aid.

“You raise your ability to get aid the more above the median that you are, whether you’re a domestic student or an international student,” Smitobol said.

The US is at risk of making a faulty assumption that our appeal can survive these small indignities that we’re putting students through

David Weeks, Sunrise International

Where to look for scholarships as an international student

Smitobol suggests looking at college websites to find merit-based scholarship opportunities. While some are open only to US residents, others, like Sahani’s scholarships at Texas State, are open to international applicants as well.

Some schools also offer scholarships specific to international students. That includes Wesleyan University’s African Scholars program, which has given full scholarships to 10 African students who apply for financial aid each year since 2023. Wesleyan also has a similar scholarship, the Freeman Asian Scholars program, for Asian students.

Africa has a growing youth population, and with it comes a large concentration of young talent and innovation, said Amin Abdul-Malik Gonzalez, the school’s vice-president and dean of admissions and financial aid. However, the high cost of a US degree – such as Wesleyan’s nearly $76,000 per year in undergraduate tuition – can be an obstacle. Gonzalez believes the scholarships not only bring talent to the school, but give domestic students a chance to learn about other cultures.

“They make it possible for all students, especially those from the United States who don’t study abroad, to engage with other cultures without leaving campus,” he said in an email.

Around 10% of Wesleyan University’s student body is international, from 64 different countries. Wesleyan University meets all demonstrated financial needs “in full” for its undergraduate international students, according to Gonzalez – which would make it one of only a handful of US schools.

Other ways to lower the cost

In addition to scholarships through schools, there are hundreds of international student scholarships through other organisations. The company Envisage International maintains a database, IEFA.org, where international students can search for scholarships across multiple host countries.

In an interview with The PIE News, Envisage’s president said the website aims to be the most comprehensive and user-friendly resource for international students seeking aid. The website allows students to filter for their native country, host country, and field of study to find scholarships best suited for them.

International students can also look for work opportunities to lower the cost of attendance. Students on an F-1 visa are allowed to work up to 20 hours per week on campus while classes are in session and up to 40 hours per week during breaks.

Sahani has worked several on-campus jobs at Texas State, including as a teacher’s assistant for a lab and a class. He says working has allowed him pay for an apartment over the summer and other expenses.

“If you are in need of money to pay housing bills, it’s good to look for a job in dining halls. Then, as they complete their courses, they can also apply to be a TA, which is what I did,” he said.

Students turning to other countries for higher education

Despite aid options being available, international students may come across other obstacles to studying abroad in the US.

Last fall, new international student enrolment in the U.S. dropped by 17%, according to the Institute of International Education. It came after President Donald Trump’s near month-long pause on visa interviews, his war against many of the nation’s most prestigious universities, and his travel ban impacting 39 countries.

Recently, the US State Department unveiled plans to halt visa processing at 30 African embassies. However, even before the Trump administration, international student advocacy groups have raised alarms about high rates of visa denials, particularly for African and Asian students, and long wait times to schedule visa interviews at embassies.

Those challenges have forced some students to look to other countries for higher education, especially countries offering financial incentives.

Over the past decade, the number of African students in Chinese universities has grown tremendously, in part because of government-funded scholarships. China has pledged to provide 50,000 full scholarships to African students, along with 60,000 fully funded training programs, under its 2025 through 2027 action plan.

China has become many African nations’ largest trading partner over the past decades. To further its economic relationship with Africa, the Chinese government is recruiting and training young African talent, said David Weeks, co-founder and chief operating officer of Sunrise International, which specializes in cross-border marketing between the U.S. and China, including for universities.

“China has taken a very holistic view of its engagement with African countries, and a big part of that is people-to-people exchanges,” he said.

Like much of the world, English is a common secondary language for students to learn in Africa, if they’re not already native English speakers. To boost recruitment, some Chinese universities have started offering degree programs entirely in English.

In addition, China’s online scholarship application portal is available in English, along with French, Arabic, and Indonesian. Currently, the website shows 3,820 scholarships, including those run by the federal government, available for English-language programs.

Making the most of Chinese scholarship opportunities

As Weeks explains, applying for Chinese scholarships often involves more notarisation and fewer personal essays compared to US scholarships.

He suggests that, before applying, students should research whether their country has a high demand for the program they’re interested in. It can often be difficult to secure a job in China if someone isn’t fluent in Mandarin Chinese.

He also cautions that universities in China often offer fewer on-campus services for international students compared to universities in Western countries. Many US schools have an international services office to help students with cultural adjustment, understanding healthcare options, and setting up a bank account. However, these services are rare for Chinese universities, which tend to have much fewer international students.

“Many universities in the UK and Australia can be as much as 30% international. There are very few universities in China that are more than 5% international,” Weeks said.

War for global talent

China is far from the only country recruiting international students. There are also government-sponsored scholarship programs in Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, Turkey, and others.

Smitobol from Ivywise said that, while many US institutions have traditionally been viewed as highly prestigious, other countries also have elite universities, where international students graduate with fewer loans.

“If schools are recognising the strength of an international population, absolutely, I think students should go where the money is and where it makes sense,” he said.

The US still hosts more international students than any other country, totalling nearly 1.2 million for the 2024/2025 school year. Weeks warns that, as more countries provide financial incentives to international students, the prestige of US schools alone won’t be enough to attract the brightest students.

“I think there’s this broader tension of which countries are going to be able to recruit the best and the brightest. I think the US is at risk of making a faulty assumption that our appeal can survive these small indignities that we’re putting students through,” he said.

title: Five Things I Wish I Knew My First Semester
summary:
My first semester as a faculty member taught me something I wish I had understood on day one: most of the stress did not come from teaching itself. It came from the absence of systems. I was making constant small decisions—how to answer student emails, when to grant an extension, what to do when a […]

The post Five Things I Wish I Knew My First Semester appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
My first semester as a faculty member taught me something I wish I had understood on day one: most of the stress did not come from teaching itself. It came from the absence of systems. I was making constant small decisions—how to answer student emails, when to grant an extension, what to do when a student disappeared, how to keep course materials organized, and how to protect research time when the week kept getting fragmented. None of those decisions seemed large in isolation, but together they created a steady drain on time and attention.

What helped was not finding a perfect method. It was building a few repeatable habits that made the semester more manageable for both my students and me. The five practices below are simple, practical, and adaptable across disciplines. They do not eliminate the learning curve of a first semester, but they do reduce unnecessary friction.

1. Create Communication Scripts Before You Need Them

Most student emails fall into a small number of categories: missed work, extension requests, confusion about instructions, grade questions, technology problems, and “I’m behind—what should I do now?” If I wrote every response from scratch, email quickly became a second job. What changed everything was creating a small bank of reusable responses.

A good script has three parts: a respectful acknowledgment, a reference to the relevant course policy or resource, and a next step. For example, instead of writing a long custom reply, I could say, “Thanks for reaching out. Please review the late-work policy in the syllabus, and then submit the assignment by the updated deadline listed in the LMS.” That kind of response is calm, clear, and consistent.

The goal is not to sound robotic. The goal is to reduce decision fatigue and improve fairness. When students receive similar guidance in similar situations, they are less likely to feel that policies are arbitrary. I also learned to send one short weekly announcement in my LMS that answered common questions before students needed to ask them: what is due, what to prioritize, and what usually causes trouble that week. Those announcements prevented many repeat emails before they ever landed in my inbox.

2. Make Expectations Explicit Early

Many first-semester problems are not really performance problems; they are expectation problems. Students often do poorly not because they are unwilling to succeed, but because they are guessing about what “good participation,” “professional communication,” or “acceptable collaboration” actually means.

One of the most useful things I did was create a single “How to succeed in this course” page. I included communication norms, participation expectations, late-work rules, where to find assignments, how quickly I respond to email, and what students should do if they fall behind. I also addressed issues that now matter in almost every class, such as responsible use of AI tools and how to distinguish collaboration from unauthorized help.

The important part is not just posting expectations once. It is revisiting them early and enforcing them gently but consistently. If a student sends an unprofessional email in week two, that is the right time to redirect them. If several students misunderstand an assignment, that is a signal to clarify the directions immediately. Small course corrections early prevent repeated negotiations later. Clear expectations are not about being rigid; they are about making the course more predictable and easier to navigate.

3. Build a Default Weekly Workflow

In a first semester, it is easy to let the calendar decide everything for you. Meetings get scheduled, student needs pop up, grading expands, and research time disappears into whatever space is left. I learned that if I did not build a default week, the week built itself around the most immediate demand.

My solution was simple: protect a few recurring blocks. I designated specific times for course prep, grading, and scholarship. Even a single 60-minute protected block was more effective than hoping I would “find time” later. I also started grading in batches. Instead of checking the LMS constantly and responding to each new submission or question as it appeared, I grouped similar tasks together. That made me faster, more focused, and more consistent in my evaluation of student work.

Another small habit helped more than I expected: I kept a running “next semester fixes” list. When I noticed an unclear instruction, an awkward assignment sequence, or a resource students kept missing, I wrote it down rather than trying to rebuild the course mid-semester. That list lowered my stress because it let me acknowledge a problem without turning it into an emergency. Sometimes the most sustainable move is not to fix everything now, but to capture it for later.

4. Ask for Mid-Semester Feedback While You Can Still Use It

End-of-term evaluations tell us how students felt after the course is over. Mid-semester feedback tells us what we can still improve while the course is in motion. Once I began using a short anonymous check-in, I found it to be one of the most efficient teaching tools I had.

I kept it to five questions: What is helping your learning? What is still unclear? Is the pacing manageable? Is the workload reasonable? What is one change that would help you succeed? Those questions provided useful information without causing survey fatigue. More importantly, they helped me identify friction points that were easy to fix: unclear instructions, too many clustered due dates, or a resource that students did not realize was available.

The real value comes from closing the loop. In the next class or announcement, I would briefly say, “Here is what I heard, here is what I am going to adjust, and here is what will stay the same.” Students responded well when they saw that feedback had a purpose. I did not need to adopt every suggestion. I just needed to show that I was listening and making thoughtful decisions. That transparency improved trust, engagement, and, ultimately, the course’s tone.

5. Learn Your Campus Referral Network Before a Problem Becomes a Crisis

One of the hardest parts of a first semester is realizing how many student issues are not purely instructional in nature. Students may struggle with attendance, accommodations, mental health concerns, financial pressure, technology barriers, conduct issues, or personal crises. New faculty often feel pressure to solve these situations on their own. That is rarely the best approach.

What helped me was learning the referral map early. I needed to know who handled disability accommodations, student conduct, counseling and wellness, academic support, Title IX concerns, library assistance, and LMS or classroom technology problems. I also needed to understand an important professional boundary: my job was not to investigate everything or become the sole support system. My job was to respond appropriately, document when needed, and connect students to the right office.

This is practical workload management as much as it is student support. When faculty know where to refer, they act more consistently and with less uncertainty. Instead of improvising under pressure, they can say, “Here is the office that can help, and here is your next step.” That helps students faster and reduces the isolation many new instructors feel when difficult situations arise.

A Final Thought

If I could go back and advise myself before that first semester began, I would not say, “Work harder.” I would say, “Build better systems sooner.” A few well-designed habits can dramatically reduce the chaos that makes new teaching feel overwhelming.

For anyone starting out, I recommend choosing one practical change this week:

Create three email scripts you know you will reuse.

Post one weekly LMS announcement template.

Draft a five-question mid-semester check-in.

Identify the three campus offices you are most likely to need.

You do not need to solve everything at once. The goal is not perfection. The goal is to build a sustainable way of teaching—one that supports students while also protecting your time, attention, and confidence.

Peter Szawranskyj holds both a bachelor’s and a master’s degree from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, where his graduate studies focused on safety and human factors. He is currently pursuing a PhD in Occupational Safety and Health at West Virginia University, with a research focus on human factors, training, and safety behavior in aviation. His academic and research interests include advanced cockpit design, cognitive science, and aviation safety systems. He currently serves as a faculty member in the Department of Aeronautical Science at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, where he teaches and mentors future aviation professionals. In addition, he serves as a faculty mentor, supporting and guiding new faculty in their professional development and instructional effectiveness. In this role, he draws on more than three decades of military and civilian aviation experience to bring a practical, safety-focused perspective to the classroom. His instruction emphasizes real-world applications of human factors, crew resource management, flight department operations, and advanced flight systems.

In addition to his academic responsibilities, Peter also serves as the Director of Aviation for a large corporate flight department. In this capacity, he oversees operations for a fleet that includes two Challenger jets and is actively involved in all aspects of flight department management, including flight operations, regulatory compliance, and safety oversight. His leadership in this role provides valuable, current industry insights that enhance his teaching and benefit his students. Peter began his flying career as an F-14 Tomcat pilot in the United States Navy. Following his service, he held various roles in the airline, charter, and corporate aviation sectors, including Safety Officer, Chief Pilot, and Director of Operations. He holds type ratings in the A320, B737, BE-300, BE-400, CL-30, CL-604, DA-50, G-IV, G-V, and MU-300.

Outside of his professional work, Peter is an avid adventurer. He enjoys scuba diving, hang gliding, and soaring in his Stemme S12 motor glider. He also volunteers with wildlife rehabilitation efforts, helping to care for injured and orphaned animals in his community.

title: Navigating research culture(s) in HE: Pracademia and professional identity
summary: by Monika Foster, Jill Dickinson and Debbie Rigby The intensification of the research agenda across higher education (HE) has sharpened questions about who participates in research, on what terms, and with what support. This is perhaps most prominent in post-1992 … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Monika Foster, Jill Dickinson and Debbie Rigby

The intensification of the research agenda across higher education (HE) has sharpened questions about who participates in research, on what terms, and with what support. This is perhaps most prominent in post-1992 institutions whose applied agenda historically called for professionals to join academia to enhance knowledge-practice links, but who are recently experiencing a shift in research intensification. Academics with practitioner experience, commonly referred to as pracademics (Volpe and Chandler, 1999), have the potential to occupy an increasingly significant, yet under-recognised position within this landscape. Entering academia from professional practice, they must simultaneously navigate unfamiliar research cultures, renegotiate their professional identities, and reconcile competing demands from the worlds of practice and scholarship (Huey and Mitchell, 2016).

In this blog, we focus on a British Academy/Leverhulme funded project (Leeds Beckett University, 2026) that explored how pracademics might renegotiate their identities as they operate within, and move between, the different working contexts presented by practice and academia (Johnson and Ellis, 2023; Huey and Mitchell, 2016). We reflect on the findings that highlight the gaps that exist within both the literature and university practices to support pracademics who work within post-1992 institutions in renegotiating their identities as they navigate the research culture within HE.

Understanding research: the practitioner-academic identity and research divide

The literature suggests that pracademics can complement a diverse faculty (Dickinson and Griffiths, 2023) by transgressing boundaries, serving as network brokers between academia and industry, and creating new channels to enhance cooperation and communication across the academic-practitioner divide (Powell et al, 2018; Panda, 2014). However, an emerging pracademic identity may take time to adjust as practitioners might simultaneously hold on to their practitioner identities whilst developing new skills and connections in academia. Institutions and external partners that achieve higher levels of practitioner-academic collaboration are more likely to be more successful (Hughes et al, 2011; Posner, 2009). Organisations with the strongest academic networks and research capacities are likely to produce wider social, community and policy impacts as well as the benefits for business (Nicolaou and Birley, 2003; Siegel et al, 2007).

Against this backdrop, we sought to explore the following three questions: What do pracademics understand by the phrase ‘research within HE’? To what extent do pracademics perceive themselves as able to engage in, and navigate, the research within HE? And What other factors do pracademics perceive as either supporting or inhibiting their potential to contribute to the research within HE?

Practitioner-academic identity and research culture

We have purposively sampled institutions that are likely to employ a significant number of pracademics and that are developing their research agenda alongside their teaching offer. Post-1992 institutions (granted university status through the Further and Higher Education Act 1992) have traditionally recruited more pracademics (Obembe, 2023) and are increasingly focused on strengthening their research alongside their teaching provision (Guthrie and Neumann, 2007). Through an online survey completed by forty-five pracademics working in post-1992 universities, we intended to build an initial picture of pracademics’ experiences by exploring understandings of research culture, confidence in engaging in research, and professional identity, which helped identify key issues for further exploration.

The survey results highlighted no single understanding or definition of what research culture meant and participants consistently described it as much more than simply undertaking research. Factors perceived to support engagement with research culture included: supportive colleagues, mentoring, collaboration, opportunities for informal knowledge exchange and access to research development opportunities. In contrast, competing workload demands, limited time, unclear pathways into research, unfamiliar academic processes, and a lack of confidence seem to inhibit engagement.

Based on the survey outcomes, we explored further pracademics’ professional identity, how they navigate research culture, what they value in research, and how they experience the changing expectations of higher education in focus groups. Focus groups’ participants were from a range of disciplines including education, business, law, social work and policy. The focus group discussions were analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006), and four interconnected themes emerged that capture pracademics’ journey and transition, starting with their professional identities, making sense of research culture, practitioners’ values, and how these values and experiences sit within a changing higher education landscape.

Theme 1: “It’s the synergy between the two”. Constructing a pracademic identity

Who am I becoming as a pracademic? Across the focus groups, we noted a recurring theme of professional identities, bringing established professional knowledge, values and experience into HE, drawing upon different aspects of themselves depending on the context. For many, their practitioner and academic identities were not experienced as separate or competing, but as closely connected. This is captured well in the words of one of the focus groups participants: “it’s the synergy between the two that makes it really interesting”, explaining that “sometimes it’s the practice that’s doing the heavy lifting and sometimes it’s the academic bit that’s doing the heavy lifting.”

Theme 2: “Learning the rules of a different game”. Navigating the hidden cultures of higher education

How do I learn to navigate the academic world? Although the research participants entered HE with substantial professional expertise, many reported feeling unexpectedly like novices when trying to grasp research culture. Research culture was described differently across the focus groups. Some participants described it as the environment in which research happens, whilst others reflected on arriving in HE with little understanding of where to begin “a little bit daunting on arrival”.These discussions suggest that engaging with research culture involves much more than learning research skills; it involves learning the language, expectations and culture of HE itself.

Theme 3: “Working with people rather than on people”. Practitioner values shaping research

What values do pracademics bring? Participants described research through the values they brought with them from professional practice. Research was described as most valuable when it remained connected to the communities and professions it sought to serve. Across the focus groups, participants consistently described their practitioner experience as shaping not only the research they wanted to undertake, but also how they understood impact. Research was valued for its ability to improve practice, support students and contribute to professional communities, research is not as an activity separate from practice, but as an extension of it.

Theme 4: When pracademic values meet institutional realities. Negotiating value within contemporary HE

What happens when those values encounter the realities of contemporary higher education? Whilst there was a strong commitment to research across the focus groups, participants also described becoming increasingly aware of what appeared to be recognised, rewarded and made visible within contemporary universities. Research outputs, funding applications and academic progression were often interpreted as indicators of what institutions value. A recurring thread throughout these discussions was participants’ growing awareness that research culture is changing, has research culture become “an empty signifier for ‘how many articles are you getting published in four-star journals?'”, whilst also asking where professional expertise, leadership and knowledge exchange fitted within this changing landscape.

Navigating research culture in a changing HE landscape

Overall, our study has shone a light on how pracademics navigate research culture within a changing HE landscape. Beyond simply identifying barriers to engagement, we explored how they establish professional identities and shape participants’ understandings of meaningful research, academic identity and the changing expectations of contemporary universities. The findings from the project suggest that these pracademics do not experience becoming academics as leaving their practitioner identities behind. They consistently describe building upon their professional knowledge, skills and values. Their practitioner identities remain central to how they understand themselves and the contribution they make within HE.

It is apparent that pracademics move between practitioner and academic perspectives depending on the context in which they are working. This flexibility strengthens their teaching, shapes the research questions they ask, and enables them to connect with students, colleagues and professional communities reflecting both worlds. Given the richness of contributions that pracademics can make in research and practice in universities, we hope that these findings might inform a broad range of stakeholders, including: policymakers, HE-related charities, senior university leadership, human resources and organisational development, research development, those who self-identify as pracademics, and those who have taken more traditional career paths.

Monika Foster is Professor of Business Education and Associate Pro Vice-Chancellor International and Educational Partnerships at Northumbria University, National Teaching Fellow and PFHEA, her research interests include leadership and change management, cross-cultural management and social capital development.

Jill Dickinson is Professor of Law and Professional Development at Leeds Law School, Leeds Beckett University, PFHEA, an Executive Coach (L7) and Solicitor (non-practising), and her research draws on creative methods to explore professional development and place-making.

Debbie Rigby is a PhD researcher at Leeds Beckett University and a former secondary school science teacher, Assistant Headteacher and teacher educator with a particular interest in research culture and professional identity in higher education.

title: Why the youth jobs crisis is becoming global
summary: Young people in much of the world face growing competition for entry-level jobs as graduate numbers rise, hiring slows and AI-driven disruption adds uncertainty to career prospects.
full_text:
The youth job crisis that first became obvious in China points to major economic and social problems that governments and businesses need to address.

Last year, unemployment, weak job prospects and a general lack of economic opportunities drove young people onto the streets in Kenya, Peru, Nepal, Indonesia and the Philippines.

This year, concerns about youth unemployment have added fuel to protests in South Africa and Morocco. In India, they helped give rise to the Cockroach Janta Party, a movement that started as a satirical social media project but quickly gained national attention.

China's youth unemployment problem

Youth unemployment refers to the share of young people, typically aged 15 to 24, who are actively seeking work but cannot find it. The rate is usually higher than overall unemployment because young people have less experience and networking opportunities, but that gap is widening in a growing number of countries.

China became an early example of the problem as university enrolment and graduate numbers grew faster than job creation, contributing to anxiety, long job searches and underemployment during a period of weaker economic growth.

In May, the official unemployment rate among ​urban 16-to 24-year-olds in ‌China was ​15.6%, according to Reuters news agency based on National Bureau of Statistics data.

While this represents the lowest level ⁠in 11 ​months, it remains three times higher than the overall unemployment rate of around 5%. Since 2023, the Chinese youth unemployment figures exclude the millions of university students, making comparisons with older data harder.

Is AI reshaping entry-level job opportunities?

China is not the only country with weak growth, slowing upward mobility, or a sense of intergenerational inequality.

In other countries, technology, sluggish hiring and rising competition have also weakened the link between a university degree and a secure white-collar career.

Besides the growing number of graduates, another factor eating away at confidence is the fear that artificial intelligence (AI) could turn into a massive entry-level job destroyer. Experts are not yet clear about its impact.

"In the UK, new postings for graduate jobs have fallen faster than for non-graduate jobs, and many of these roles are highly exposed to AI," said Golo Henseke, an associate professor in applied economics at University College London.

His research has shown that "where firms have taken up AI faster, employment of 15-to 24-year-olds has grown more slowly, while prime-age employment holds up." But for now, the AI-effect is small compared to the regular business cycle.

Sara Elder, a youth employment expert at the Geneva-based International Labour Organization (ILO), agrees. AI may be one of the current drivers of stagnating youth employment, but she considers other factors more important.

Right now, economies are not dynamic and job creation is just not keeping pace with the number of young people seeking jobs, says Elder.

"This is then exacerbated by the tendency of employers to raise hiring criteria in ways that make it more difficult for young people with little job experience to get their foot in the door," said Elder.

What type of jobs are impacted where?

Without these entry-level jobs, young people may never get the experience they need for better jobs. Consequences could be lower consumption, lower home ownership rates and delayed family formation — not to mention widespread frustration.

Currently across Europe, there is no broad youth jobs crisis, says Henseke, who specializes in education, labor markets and human resources.

Since 2022, the share of young people not in employment, education, or training has increased in only a handful of European countries like Austria and Germany and fallen in much of southern Europe.

"Youth unemployment is not new to Europe either," said Henseke. "It was severe after the financial crisis, and the biggest improvements since have been in the countries that struggled most then."

But the ILO found that between 2023 and 2025 youth unemployment rates rose in eight of the world's 11 regions, like East Asia, North America (the US and Canada), Southeast Asia and the Pacific.

Opportunities for young people have declined in manufacturing, construction and the service sectors, in particular.

"Jobs for young people in high-skilled knowledge-based technical areas, like science, engineering, health and information and communication technologies, have fared better, showing continued growth in most countries," said Elder.

What can be done about entry-level jobs?

In Germany, a survey this spring by consultancy EY found that students are much less optimistic about finding suitable work after graduation than they were two years ago. Job security now also ranks ahead of salary as their top priority when choosing an employer.

This leaves lots of room for improvement. Policymakers and employers will need to make big investments to create decent jobs and "support young people's school-to-work transitions," said Elder.

Golo Henseke is cautious about blaming young people's skills. "It is very unlikely that today's graduates are less capable than those who left education just a few years ago, and the skills employers want have not changed overnight."

"More than anything, what would help is economic growth," concluded Henseke.

title: Cybergrooming-Prozess: Er missbrauchte 21 Mädchen online – Mann zu Haft verurteilt
summary: Ein 33-Jähriger chattet mit Kindern – und fordert sie auf, ihm pornographische Inhalte zu schicken. Nun muss er mehr als drei Jahre hinter Gitter. Damit blieb das Gericht deutlich unter der Forderung der Staatsanwaltschaft.

Cybergrooming-Prozess :

Er missbrauchte 21 Mädchen online – Mann zu Haft verurteilt

21.07.2026, 15:38Lesezeit: 2 Min.

Die Opfer des 33-Jährigen kommen aus ganz Deutschland (Symbolbild).dpa

Ein 33-Jähriger chattet mit Kindern – und fordert sie auf, ihm pornographische Inhalte zu schicken. Nun muss er mehr als drei Jahre hinter Gitter. Damit blieb das Gericht deutlich unter der Forderung der Staatsanwaltschaft.

Ein 33-Jähriger aus der Nähe von Heidelberg hat über das Internet mehr als 20 Mädchen sexuell missbraucht und ist dafür zu drei Jahren und zehn Monaten Haft verurteilt worden. Das Landgericht Heidelberg sah es als erwiesen an, dass der Mann die Opfer im Alter von acht bis 13 Jahren dazu gebracht hatte, ihm von sich selbst angefertigte pornografische Inhalte zu schicken. Die Mädchen kommen aus ganz Deutschland, wie eine Sprecherin des Gerichts sagte.

Der Mann aus dem Rhein-Neckar-Kreis wurde demnach wegen eines Falles von sexuellem Missbrauch von Kindern verurteilt sowie wegen 30 Fällen von sexuellem Missbrauch von Kindern ohne Körperkontakt und der Herstellung von kinderpornographischen Inhalten. Er hatte die Taten laut Gericht gestanden und den Kindern damit Aussagen in dem Prozess erspart. Das Urteil ist nicht rechtskräftig.

F.A.Z.-Artikel häufiger in Ihren Suchergebnissen sehen

F.A.Z. bei Google bevorzugen

Kontakte über Whatsapp und Snapchat

Laut Gericht kontaktierte der Mann zwischen 2023 und 2025 zahlreiche Mädchen über die Messenger-Dienste Whatsapp und Snapchat. Dabei habe er den Mädchen vorgespielt, er sei Jugendlicher oder Heranwachsender. Dann habe er die Mädchen dazu aufgefordert, ihm von sich selbst erstellte pornografische Inhalte zuzuschicken.

Der Mann habe auch von sich erstellte pornografische Inhalte an die Mädchen geschickt, vor allem Videos, wie das Landgericht mitteilte. Schließlich hätten 21 Mädchen dem heute 33-Jährigen von sich selbst angefertigte kinderpornografische Fotos und Videos übersandt. In einem weiteren Fall sei es beim Versuch geblieben.

Anklage durch das Cybercrime-Zentrum

Die Ermittler kamen dem Mann laut Gericht auf die Spur, nachdem Eltern eines Opfers Anzeige erstattet hatten. Er wurde laut einer früheren Mitteilung im vergangenen November festgenommen und saß seither in Untersuchungshaft. Das Cybercrime-Zentrum Baden-Württemberg hatte den Mann angeklagt. Es gehört zur Generalstaatsanwaltschaft Karlsruhe.

Mit dem Urteil blieb das Landgericht Heidelberg deutlich unter der Forderung der Staatsanwaltschaft, die sich für eine Haftstrafe von vier Jahren und zehn Monaten ausgesprochen hatte. Die Verteidigung hatte auf eine Haftstrafe von maximal drei Jahren und sechs Monaten plädiert, wie die Gerichtssprecherin sagte.

He abused 21 girls online – man sentenced to prison

July 21, 2026, 3:38 p.m. Reading time: 2 min.

The 33-year-old's victims come from all over Germany (symbolic image).dpa

A 33-year-old chats with children - and asks them to send him pornographic content. Now he has to spend more than three years behind bars. The court thus fell well short of the public prosecutor's demands.

A 33-year-old from near Heidelberg sexually abused more than 20 girls over the Internet and was sentenced to three years and ten months in prison. The Heidelberg regional court found it proven that the man had persuaded the victims, aged eight to 13, to send him pornographic content that they had made themselves. The girls come from all over Germany, a spokeswoman for the court said.

The man from the Rhein-Neckar district was convicted of one case of sexual abuse of children as well as 30 cases of sexual abuse of children without physical contact and the production of child pornography content. According to the court, he confessed to the crimes and thus spared the children from having to testify in the trial. The judgment is not final.

F.A.Z. prefer on Google

Contacts via Whatsapp and Snapchat

According to the court, the man contacted numerous girls between 2023 and 2025 via the messenger services Whatsapp and Snapchat. He pretended to the girls that he was a teenager or an adolescent. He then asked the girls to send him pornographic content that they had created themselves.

The man also sent pornographic content he had created to the girls, especially videos, the district court said. Ultimately, 21 girls sent the now 33-year-old child pornography photos and videos they had made themselves. In another case it remained an attempt.

Charged by the Cybercrime Center

According to the court, investigators tracked down the man after parents of a victim filed a complaint. According to an earlier statement, he was arrested last November and has been in custody ever since. The Baden-Württemberg Cybercrime Center had charged the man. It belongs to the Karlsruhe Public Prosecutor's Office.

With the verdict, the Heidelberg regional court fell well short of the public prosecutor's demands, which had advocated a prison sentence of four years and ten months. The defense had pleaded for a maximum prison sentence of three years and six months, as the court spokeswoman said.

title: Chef(fe) de projet – Département Économie

full_text:
Le Haut-commissariat à la Stratégie et au Plan

Le Haut-commissariat à la Stratégie et au Plan est un organisme autonome, rattaché aux services du Premier ministre, d’expertise et d’analyse prospective sur les grands sujets sociaux et économiques. Il contribue à orienter les choix des décideurs publics et à éclairer le débat public en France.

À ce titre, il produit des travaux d’évaluation, de prospective et de planification sur l’ensemble des politiques publiques, sous forme notamment de notes, de documents de travail et de rapports.

Son organisation s’articule autour de quatre départements thématiques : Économie ; Travail, emploi compétences ; Société et politiques sociales ; et Environnement.

Le département Économie

Le département Économie a pour mission d’analyser les moteurs d’une croissance soutenable à moyen et long terme et de formuler des propositions de politique publiques en la matière. Il exerce également un rôle transversal de veille sur les questions économiques de plus court terme et d’appui aux travaux menés au sein du Haut-commissariat en lien avec les priorités nationales.

L’équipe concentre ses travaux sur les politiques économiques : finances publiques, politiques d’innovation, politiques commerciales, soutien à la productivité et à la compétitivité, conditions de la croissance des entreprises, transition bas carbone, développement de filières industrielles, notamment dans le secteur de la défense ou du numérique.

Dans ce cadre, le département mobilise des approches complémentaires, à la fois macroéconomiques et microéconomiques, en s’appuyant sur les travaux académiques, la modélisation et l’expertise des acteurs économiques afin d’éclairer ses analyses et recommandations.

Missions

En tant que chef(fe) de projet, vous contribuerez à la conception et à la réalisation des travaux d’analyse, d’évaluation et de prospective du département Économie.

Vous interviendrez sur des projets portant sur des problématiques économiques variées, en fonction du programme de travail du Haut-commissariat et des priorités de l’action publique (finances publiques, politiques d’innovation, développement de filières industrielles notamment dans le secteur du numérique, etc.).

Vous participerez directement à la production de notes, de documents de travail, et de rapports administratifs. Vous veillerez à inscrire ces productions dans une perspective stratégique et prospective, afin d’éclairer la décision publique sur les grands enjeux économiques.

Vous serez amené(e) à mobiliser des approches quantitatives et qualitatives, en vous appuyant sur les données économiques disponibles, les travaux académiques, les analyses économiques, ainsi que sur l’expertise des administrations, institutions internationales, entreprises, fédérations professionnelles et acteurs académiques.

Vous contribuerez également à la valorisation de vos travaux, notamment à travers l’organisation ou la participation à des colloques, conférences, groupes de travail, auditions et interventions publiques.

Dans ce cadre, vous serez en interaction régulière avec de nombreux partenaires : chefs de projets au sein du département et des autres départements du Haut-commissariat, administrations, experts académiques, cabinets ministériels, institutions européennes et internationales, représentants du monde économique et organisations professionnelles.

Profil recherché

• Vous êtes titulaire d’un doctorat et/ou d’un diplôme de grande école ou d’un Master 2 en économie, ou disposez d’une formation et d’une expérience équivalentes.

• Vous justifiez d’une expérience professionnelle dans une administration publique, une banque centrale, une organisation internationale, une institution européenne, un centre de recherche, un think tank, ou à l’université, sur des sujets liés au commerce international.

• Vous disposez de solides compétences en économie, d’une culture économique générale et maîtrisez les principaux concepts et outils de l’analyse macroéconomique et microéconomique, et êtes capable de produire des analyses rigoureuses sur des sujets complexes.

• Vous êtes à l’aise avec l’analyse de données économiques, ainsi qu’avec l’exploitation de sources statistiques nationales, européennes et internationales.

• Vous disposez de solides compétences en interprétation, synthèse et mise en valeur de résultats statistiques et économétriques.

• Vous maîtrisez des logiciels et langages d’analyse de données tels que Python, R ou STATA.

• Vous faites preuve de vision stratégique et de capacités de proposition et de conseil en matière de politiques publiques, en alliant créativité, rigueur analytique et sens du réalisme.

• Vous êtes à l’aise dans un environnement pluridisciplinaire, ouvert à la confrontation des idées, et appréciez le travail en équipe.

• Vous possédez d’excellentes capacités d’analyse et de synthèse, et savez articuler travaux de recherche, expertise économique et enjeux opérationnels.

• Vous êtes en mesure d’intervenir à toutes les étapes d’un projet, comme pilote ou contributeur, et disposez de solides capacités rédactionnelles pour traiter des sujets complexes, y compris dans des délais contraints.

• Vous êtes à l’aise à l’oral et capable de présenter vos travaux auprès de partenaires variés, ainsi qu’à des publics non spécialistes.

• Vous souhaitez vous engager au service de l’action publique et contribuer à l’amélioration des politiques publiques en France.

• La maîtrise de l’anglais, à l’oral comme à l’écrit, est indispensable.

Informations complémentaires

title: Extended learning: apprendere facendo nell’era dell’AI
summary:
La trasformazione digitale e l’intelligenza artificiale stanno cambiando il modo in cui le aziende sviluppano competenze. L’extended learning propone un modello formativo basato su esperienza, collaborazione e ambienti immersivi, con applicazioni già adottate da grandi organizzazioni internazionali

L'articolo Extended learning: apprendere facendo nell’era dell’AI proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
Negli ultimi anni il mondo del lavoro è cambiato più velocemente di quanto molte organizzazioni fossero preparate ad affrontare. Trasformazione digitale, intelligenza artificiale e continua evoluzione delle competenze stanno imponendo alle aziende una nuova sfida: apprendere in modo rapido, efficace e continuo.

Secondo numerose ricerche internazionali, una quota crescente delle competenze richieste oggi sarà diversa nel giro di pochi anni. Questo significa che la formazione diventerà sempre di più una leva strategica per garantire competitività, innovazione e capacità di adattamento.

Eppure, proprio mentre gli investimenti in formazione aumentano, emerge una domanda cruciale: quanto di ciò che impariamo durante un corso riusciamo davvero ad applicare nel lavoro quotidiano?

Dal digital learning alla sfida delle competenze applicate

Per oltre vent’anni l’e-learning prima e poi il digital learning hanno rappresentato un supporto ad integrazione della formazione in aula rendendo i contenuti scalabili e disponibili in qualsiasi momento. I format didattico-multimediali hanno avuto una normale evoluzione ma ormai da tempo sono rimasti in una condizione di stasi e capaci di trasferire nella maggior parte dei casi conoscenze da un sistema a una persona.

Sapere però non significa saper fare. Completare un corso in versione digitale non garantisce l’acquisizione di una competenza. E soprattutto, la semplice esposizione ai contenuti non sempre genera coinvolgimento, partecipazione e cambiamento dei comportamenti.

Cosa ci insegnano neuroscienze e ricerca

Le neuroscienze ci aiutano a comprendere il motivo.

Il neuroscienziato Endel Tulving ha dimostrato l’importanza della memoria episodica, ovvero la capacità di ricordare esperienze vissute direttamente (episodi). Tendiamo infatti a ricordare ciò che abbiamo sperimentato rispetto a contesti puramente semantici.

Anche il luogo e il contesto in cui avviene l’apprendimento, pertanto, svolge un ruolo determinante. Le ricerche che hanno portato al Premio Nobel per la Medicina assegnato a John O’Keefe e ai coniugi Moser hanno evidenziato come il cervello utilizzi specifici neuroni chiamati neuroni GPS per orientarsi nello spazio e costruire mappe cognitive ed esperienze spaziali che facilitano memorizzazione e apprendimento.

A questo si aggiunge il contributo dei neuroni specchio individuati dal gruppo di ricerca guidato da Giacomo Rizzolatti, che favoriscono l’apprendimento attraverso l’osservazione e l’azione.

In altre parole, apprendiamo meglio quando viviamo un’esperienza, quando interagiamo in modo collaborativo con altri all’interno di un luogo specifico e quando possiamo mettere in pratica ciò che stiamo imparando.

I dati confermano questa direzione anche attraverso una ricerca di PwC sull’Immersive Learning: livelli di coinvolgimento e concentrazione significativamente superiori (X 3,75) rispetto alla formazione tradizionale, tempi di apprendimento più rapidi (X 4) e una maggiore sicurezza (+ 275%) nell’applicazione delle competenze acquisite.

Extended learning: l’evoluzione della formazione digitale

È in questo contesto che nasce l’Extended Learning: un nuovo modello di formazione digitale multimodale – fruibile da desktop, mobile e visori VR – il cui obiettivo è quello di creare le condizioni per permettere alle persone di apprendere attraverso il learning by doing, l’interazione, la partecipazione attiva e il collaborative learning.

In questo modello “Extended Learning”, l’apprendimento avviene all’interno di ambienti digitali tridimensionali condivisi in cui le persone possono agire e collaborare real-time, confrontarsi e sperimentare situazioni realistiche. Inoltre, integrando intelligenza artificiale e immersive learning, l’esperienza viene potenziata, rendendola più coinvolgente, contestualizzata e vicina alle modalità con cui sviluppiamo competenze nella vita reale.

Per le Direzioni Risorse Umane questo significa avere la grande opportunità offerta dalle tecnologie per ripensare e potenziare onboarding, upskilling e reskilling e competenze tecniche in modo più efficace e anche più al passo delle nuove generazioni.

La vera evoluzione della formazione digitale consiste nel progettare esperienze capaci di trasformare conoscenza in competenze concrete e immediatamente applicabili. Perché nel lavoro di oggi occorre essere in grado di agire, decidere e adattarsi.

Immersive learning nelle organizzazioni internazionali

L’immersive learning rappresenta oggi una metodologia formativa consolidata, adottata da molte organizzazioni internazionali per lo sviluppo delle competenze.

Amazon rappresenta uno dei casi più significativi: attraverso la Driver Academy, il gruppo ha introdotto programmi di formazione basati su simulazioni immersive per la preparazione degli autisti addetti alle consegne. Oltre 300.000 persone sono state coinvolte in percorsi che consentono di affrontare scenari realistici in totale sicurezza. I risultati evidenziano un aumento della retention dell’apprendimento e una riduzione dei tempi necessari per rendere operative le nuove risorse.

Anche il settore dell’aviazione sta investendo in questa direzione. Emirates ha sviluppato la piattaforma immersiva MIRA (Mixed Reality Immersive Learning Application), coinvolgendo oltre 23.000 membri dell’equipaggio nella formazione relativa alla sicurezza e alla gestione delle emergenze. Grazie a esperienze realistiche e interattive, il personale può esercitarsi più volte in procedure complesse, mantenendo elevati standard formativi a livello globale.

Un ulteriore esempio arriva da DHL, che ha introdotto soluzioni di realtà aumentata per supportare la formazione e l’attività operativa nei magazzini. Attraverso smart glasses e istruzioni digitali contestualizzate, gli operatori possono apprendere procedure e processi direttamente sul campo. Questi progetti hanno evidenziato incrementi di produttività fino al 37% rispetto ai metodi tradizionali, oltre a una riduzione degli errori e a un onboarding più rapido delle nuove risorse.
